title: Five Signs Your Brand Is Holding You Back
description: Is your own website the reason the deal stalled? Five symptoms we see in every founder call — and what each one is really telling you.
content:
Nobody books a call to say their brand is broken. They book a call because the deals are stalling, the deck feels embarrassing to send, and the site does not sound like the company they actually built. Here is what that usually means.

1. You explain what you do twice

Once with the words on the site, then again on the call — properly this time. If the second explanation is always the good one, the site is not doing its job. The fix is rarely more copy. It is deciding which single sentence you are willing to lead with, and cutting the four that hedge it.

2. Your best customers found you anyway

Referrals are wonderful and they hide everything. A brand that only works when a trusted human vouches for it first is not a brand, it is a warm introduction with a logo attached. The test is what happens to a stranger who lands cold at 11pm.

If the deal only closes after you get on the call, your brand is a bottleneck wearing a nice typeface.

3. The deck and the site disagree

Different headline, different colours, different promise. This happens because the deck gets updated for every pitch and the site gets updated never. It reads to a buyer as a company still arguing with itself — and buyers are extremely good at noticing that.

4. Every new page is a small crisis

If shipping a pricing page needs a designer, a debate, and two weeks, you do not have a system — you have a set of one-off artefacts. A real brand system makes the twentieth asset as easy as the first:

  • Type and spacing decided once, not re-litigated per page
  • Components your engineers can reach for without asking
  • Rules written down in the place the work actually happens

5. You have stopped looking at it

The most reliable signal of all. When a founder will not open their own homepage in a meeting, they already know. The embarrassment is information — it is just information nobody wants to write down.

So what now?

None of these are design problems, exactly. They are decision problems that show up as design. That is why we start every engagement with a week of discovery and hard questions rather than a mood board: the brand is the output, but the decisions are the work.

title: Why We Design in Figma and Finish in Tailwind
description: The handoff meeting is a negotiation nobody wins. Here's how we deleted it — and what changed for the engineers on the other side.
content:
For years the end of a project looked the same: a tidy Figma file, a call to walk through it, and a slow realisation over the next six weeks that what shipped was a cover version of what we drew. So we stopped handing off.

The handoff is where the design goes to die

Not because engineers are careless — because a static file cannot answer questions. What happens at 900px? What does this do while it loads? What if the name is forty characters? A Figma frame answers none of that, so every one of those decisions gets made again, quickly, by someone who was not in the room when the first one was made.

Multiply that by a few hundred small decisions and you get a site that is recognisably the design, and unmistakably not it.

Figma is for deciding. Tailwind is for building.

We still design in Figma, because it is the fastest place on earth to be wrong. Ten directions in an afternoon, thrown away by dinner. That is the job.

But once a direction is real, we stop drawing it and start building it. The design system lands as tokens and components, not as a page of specs:

  • Type, spacing, and colour become theme variables — one source, not a swatch to eyeball
  • Components ship as markup your team already knows how to read
  • The edge cases get decided while we are still the ones holding them

Your engineers get components, not screenshots — and the handoff meeting stops being a negotiation.

What actually changed

Three things, consistently. Launches got faster, because the last mile was already walked. Reviews got calmer, because we were arguing about the real thing in a real browser instead of about a picture of it. And the work stopped drifting after we left, because the rules lived in the codebase rather than in our heads.

The catch

It only works if the designers can actually write the markup. That is a hiring constraint, not a process one, and it is the main reason we have stayed four people. A design engineer who can take a direction from sketch to production is rare, and worth more than three of anything else.

title: The Six-Week Brand, and Why It Works
description: Long engagements don't make better brands, they make tired ones. What a six-week sprint forces you to decide — and why that's the point.
content:
Six weeks is not a discount. It is a constraint we picked on purpose, because the alternative — the six-month brand — fails in a way that is very hard to see while it is happening.

What long engagements actually buy

More rounds. Not more clarity, more rounds. The extra months get spent revisiting decisions that were already good in week three, because there is time to revisit them and nobody wants to be the person who says stop.

By month four the work is not better, it is just more agreed with. Those are different things, and only one of them shows up in the launch.

A shipped eight is worth more than a stalled ten.

What the deadline forces

A hard date turns opinions into decisions. It also changes who shows up: when everyone knows there are six weeks, the founder comes to the calls, and the calls are about the thing rather than about scheduling the next call.

The shape is always roughly the same:

  1. Week one — discovery. Interviews, teardowns, and the uncomfortable questions. You leave with a positioning line you can repeat.
  2. Weeks two and three — direction. One real direction, in the browser, not a mood board. We iterate on it in public.
  3. Weeks four and five — the system. Type, colour, components, and the rules that keep it honest.
  4. Week six — ship. Live, measured, and yours.

When it does not work

We are not precious about this. Six weeks fails when the decision-maker cannot make the calls in week one, when the product is still changing underneath us, or when there are four stakeholders who each need to win something. In those cases the constraint just relocates the pain, and we would rather say so on the intro call than in week five.

The part nobody expects

Clients almost never ask for more time at the end. They ask what is next — which is the whole point. The launch is the midpoint, not the finish line, and a studio that is still there in month three is worth more than one that was there for month three.
